member.name: T:JCass_Economics.Optimisers.BCAOptimiseBase
member.summary: Shared machinery for the three heuristic BCA optimisation methods: preparing each element's choices, budget arithmetic, and repeating a selection pass until it settles.
member.remarks:
The problem is a multiple-choice knapsack - at most one project per element, within a budget, maximising benefit - and all three methods are heuristics for it. They are more alike than their names suggest: all rank on the incremental benefit-cost ratio and all build from the bottom up, differing only in which projects they may consider and in what order they walk them.
Read docs/bca-optimisation-methods.md before changing anything here, rather than reconstructing the intent from the code. It covers what each method is for, how they differ, and what they will and will not do. This class deliberately carries no second copy of that explanation.
A derived class supplies one selection pass as and calls from its constructor. It must not override , which owns the repeat-until-settled loop.

member.name: M:JCass_Economics.Optimisers.BCAOptimiseBase.GetOptimalCandidates(System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary{System.String,System.Double},System.Boolean,System.String)
member.summary: Selects projects within the budget, repeating the selection pass until one changes nothing.
member.param: Budget by treatment category, or the single monolithic entry.
True when every category draws on one shared pot.
Key of that pot, or null when not monolithic.
member.returns: The selected projects, at most one per element.
member.remarks:
Why more than one pass. All three optimisers walk each element's projects in ascending cost and never rewind, so an upgrade refused for want of budget is never reconsidered. With per-category budgets that loses money: when an element is upgraded from a treatment in one budget category to one in another, it stops drawing on the first category and that money is freed. An upgrade on some other element, refused earlier because the category was full, may now fit comfortably - and before 2026-08-17 nothing went back for it. See the review document's finding P4.2.
So a pass is repeated until it changes nothing, with each element's walk rewound to the project it currently holds beforehand, which re-offers exactly the upgrades that were refused.
This terminates. A pass only ever adds a project to an element that had none, or replaces one with a dearer project further along the same list, so any pass that changes the selection strictly increases total benefit. There are finitely many selections, so no selection can recur, so the sequence of changing passes is finite. is a backstop against that argument being wrong, not part of it.
A single monolithic pot cannot free money between categories, so there is nothing to reclaim and the second pass simply changes nothing. The cost of iterating in that case is one extra pass.

member.name: M:JCass_Economics.Optimisers.BCAOptimiseBase.SetupCollections
member.summary: Builds the per-element project lists the selection works from. Derived classes must call this before any selection happens.
member.remarks:
The order of the steps matters and none is interchangeable: group by element, trim each element to a front, drop elements the trim emptied, then inject do-nothings, sort by cost and compute the incremental ratios. Trimming before injecting is what stops a caller-supplied do-nothing being dropped by the front and never replaced.
This writes and the deltas onto the caller's own project objects, so a candidate list cannot be shared between two optimisers.

member.summary: Records, for every project on every element, what it costs and delivers over the project below it.
member.remarks:
Nothing reads or . The values are written here and consumed nowhere in the framework, in any client domain model, or in the tests - selection runs on instead. They are kept because they are public on and cost little.
The method is not dead, though: its ascending-cost check is a live guard against an element's projects being handed to the selection out of order, which would silently corrupt every incremental ratio.

member.name: M:JCass_Economics.Optimisers.BCAOptimiseBase.AddDoNothingsAndSortOnCost(System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary{System.Int32,System.Boolean})
member.summary: Gives every element a do-nothing option if it lacks one, orders its projects by ascending cost, and computes each project's incremental benefit-cost ratio.
member.param: Which elements already carry an absolute do-nothing, by element index.
member.remarks:
The injected do-nothing is what lets an element be left untreated: it sits at index 0 after the sort, which is where every walk starts. It is never returned as a selection.
Ordering by cost is not cosmetic - the incremental ratios computed here are slopes between adjacent projects, so they are only meaningful against a cost-ordered list.

member.name: M:JCass_Economics.Optimisers.BCAOptimiseBase.TrimElementProjectsToParetoFrontOnly
member.summary: Reduces each element's projects to its Pareto front - used by bca-greedy and bca-egalitarian.
member.remarks: Keeps every project offering more benefit than anything cheaper, so the element retains its full ladder of sensible choices including ones with diminishing slopes. Contrast . See docs/bca-optimisation-methods.md section 2.

member.name: M:JCass_Economics.Optimisers.BCAOptimiseBase.RemoveElementKeysWithoutProjects
member.summary: Drops elements whose trim left them with nothing to choose between.
member.remarks:
The test used to be elemProjects is null, which never fires: the trim assigns either the list returned by GetParetoFront or GetDecreasingIBCRFront(...) ?? new List<ProjectBase>(), so the value is never null - it is empty. The method therefore removed nothing at all.
Fixing it changes no selection. An element left with an empty list still gets an injected do-nothing, still sits at index 0, and is immediately exhausted by every optimiser's index < Count - 1 test, so it could never contribute a pick. What it saves is the pointless work of carrying it.

member.name: M:JCass_Economics.Optimisers.BCAOptimiseBase.TrimElementProjectsToDecreasingIBCROnly
member.summary: Reduces each element's projects to its decreasing-IBCR front - used by bca-ibcr only.
member.remarks: A strictly smaller set than the Pareto front: it keeps only the projects on the convex hull of the element's options, the ones a buyer facing diminishing returns would ever stop at. See docs/bca-optimisation-methods.md section 2.

member.name: M:JCass_Economics.Optimisers.BCAOptimiseBase.GetSpendingForBudgetCategory(System.Collections.Generic.List{JCass_Economics.BaseClasses.ProjectBase},System.String,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Totals what the current selection spends against one budget.
member.param: The projects selected so far.
Category to total, ignored when the budget is monolithic.
True when every category draws on one shared pot.
member.remarks:
Recomputed from the selection on every call rather than tracked, which is why the budget dictionary is never decremented anywhere in this class.
Per-category spending is not monotone. Upgrading an element from a treatment in one category to one in another removes its cost from the first category's total, so a figure returned here can fall between calls. That is what makes a single selection pass insufficient - see and finding P4.2 in the review document.

member.name: M:JCass_Economics.Optimisers.BCAOptimiseBase.CanSwopProjectOnElement(JCass_Economics.BaseClasses.ProjectBase,JCass_Economics.BaseClasses.ProjectBase,System.Double,System.Double,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Decides whether a candidate project can be taken for an element, given what has already been spent and the budget the candidate draws on.
member.param: Project currently assigned to this element, or null when it has none yet.
Project being considered in its place.
Spending already committed against .
Budget available to .
True when every treatment category draws on one shared pot.
member.remarks:
Replacing a project frees the money it was consuming - but only if that money is part of to begin with. That is the entire rule:
A monolithic budget is a single pot, so the outgoing project's cost is always in the count, whatever category it carried.
With per-category budgets it is in the count only when the outgoing project drew on the same category as the incoming one.
Deciding this on the categories alone - as this method did until 2026-08-17 - is correct for per-category budgets and wrong for a monolithic one, where it double-counts the project being removed and refuses upgrades that fit comfortably. Greedy and egalitarian felt it on every upgrade, because for them every upgrade is a swap. Nothing over-spends as a result, so no budget check can see it: the only symptom is an under-spent budget, which reads as a modelling result rather than as a defect. See the review document's finding P4.1.

member.name: T:JCass_Economics.Optimisers.BCAOptimiseConvexFront
member.summary: The standard BCA optimisation: buy the steepest increments available anywhere on the network, in one pass down a globally ranked list. Selected by the bca-ibcr setting.
member.remarks:
Note the name mismatch - the setup value is bca-ibcr but the class is BCAOptimiseConvexFront. This is the method to reach for by default, and the closest of the three to the textbook approach for a multiple-choice knapsack.
It differs from the other two in both respects that matter: it trims each element to the decreasing-IBCR front rather than the full Pareto front, and it walks one globally sorted list once instead of re-evaluating after every purchase. See docs/bca-optimisation-methods.md sections 2 and 3.

member.name: T:JCass_Economics.Optimisers.BCAOptimiseEgalitarian
member.summary: Optimisation that spreads treatment across as many elements as it can, rather than concentrating spend on the elements with the steepest benefit curves. Selected by the bca-egalitarian setting.
member.remarks:
It ranks on the incremental benefit-cost ratio like the other two; what makes it egalitarian is the shape of the search, not the ranking. Each round offers every element its next increment before any element is considered for a second, so coverage wins over total benefit.
Choose it when treating more assets matters more than maximising benefit. See docs/bca-optimisation-methods.md section 3.
